READING THE SPOT MAP

Small spots,
different stories.

Choose an oxide, then click a numbered spot. Its colour shows the reported concentration at that point. The readout below the image gives its value, calibration RMSEP and shot standard deviation; the selected-measurement panel has the full composition.

Repeated laser shots at one location are combined in the published product. They do not create additional image pixels.

Image examples are independent of the search and sol filters. Their colours use the current filter’s scale; values beyond its limits use the end colours. Unmeasured areas carry no inferred chemistry. Grey markers have no matched composition. Markers are enlarged for interaction and do not show the physical laser footprints.

SELECTED SPOT / CHEMICAL CONTEXT

Choose a measurement

These bulk-spot ratios do not give mineral fractions, hydration, iron oxidation state, or organic abundance. Dust, mixed grains, glass, salts and calibration error can produce overlapping compositions.

Published ternary approach · Clavé et al. (2023)
Calculation & interpretation

Each oxide estimate is converted to cation moles per nominal 100 g: n(Si) = SiO₂ / 60.0843; n(Al) = 2 Al₂O₃ / 101.9613; n(Fe) = FeOₜ / 71.844; n(Mg) = MgO / 40.3044; n(Ca) = CaO / 56.0774; n(Na) = 2 Na₂O / 61.9789; n(K) = 2 K₂O / 94.1960. The ternary axes are Si + Al, Ca + Na + K, and Fe + Mg, normalized only for plotting their proportions. The original oxide values and totals stay unchanged.

Reference diamonds are ideal stoichiometries: feldspar, low-Ca pyroxene, diopside, olivine and SiO₂. Distance to these points is not a mineral classifier. For a single pure phase, Al/Si ranges from 1/3 in alkali feldspar to 1 in anorthite; (Ca + Fe + Mg)/Si is 1 for common pyroxenes and 2 for olivine. Mixtures and non-silicate minerals break this simple interpretation. Bulk Mg# = 100 Mg/(Mg + total Fe) assumes all measured Fe is included; it is not a ferrous-iron measurement.

Ratios are calculated only when their required values are finite and nonnegative and their denominator is positive. Missing or negative published estimates are retained in the source table, but are excluded from these derived ratios. No ratio confidence interval is computed because the oxide covariance is unavailable. Beyssac et al. (2023) provides a worked example of interpreting LIBS with petrography and other instruments.

How to read the data

From a flash of light to a map of chemical composition.

01Laser pulse

A focused pulse interacts with the target.

02Plasma light

Excited atoms and ions emit light.

03Calibration

A trained model estimates major oxides.

04Context

Images and rover metadata locate the observation.

What the colours mean

The colours represent published major-oxide concentration estimates from the NASA Planetary Data System. They are not raw emission intensities, mineral identifications, or abundance estimates for every pixel in an image. FeOT reports total iron expressed as FeO; it does not determine the iron oxidation state.

Two missions, two calibrations

ChemCam and SuperCam have separate calibration models, sampling histories, and observing geometries. The same oxide names permit exploration across both missions, but an apparent difference can reflect more than geology. This explorer keeps each mission’s measurements and reported uncertainties intact.

Rover and image positions

The geographical map uses archive rover-position matches. Many laser targets were metres away from the rover. Image overlays use archived annotations or digitized centres of published annotation marks, as stated for each image. Neither is a complete three-dimensional reconstruction of a rock surface.

Sampling and uncertainty

LIBS rasters sample discrete locations. This explorer does not interpolate a chemical surface between them. Totals are preserved as reported and may differ from 100%. Missing estimates stay missing; calibration targets are excluded by default. Quality flags are retained for inspection rather than silently discarded.
